extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/economics; readers interested in consumption, taste, and cultural theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of how economic motives (conspicuous waste, honorific utility, conspicuous leisure) shape canons of taste, beauty, and dress; uses examples from material culture, book-making, and apparel to show selective social effects. Useful for evaluating cultural artifacts or constructing theory about consumption and status signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as facility of apperception
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of form is a question of facility of apperception: an object is beautiful insofar as the mind readily unfolds its apperceptive activity in the directions which the object affords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: aesthetic appreciation depends on habitual cognitive tendencies; long habituation adapts physiological structure and shapes what is perceived as beautiful. This frames aesthetic judgment as partly conditioned by learned perceptual habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic beauty (adequacy to purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic interest enters into beauty as a suggestion or expression of adequacy to a purpose — a manifest and readily inferable subservience to the life process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For objects of use, 'neat and unambiguous suggestion of its office and its efficiency' best serves economic beauty. Anti-pattern: ornamentation that conceals function undermines genuine economic beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple and unadorned articles are aesthetically best among objects of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Among objects of use the simple and unadorned article is aesthetically the best (from the standpoint of economic beauty/serviceability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But pecuniary canons of reputability often reject inexpensive simplicity, producing practical compromises where objects appear ornate to signal expense rather than optimized serviceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty as surrogate for beauty under pecuniary pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: When canons of beauty are circumvented by the need for reputably wasteful expenditure, novelty operates as an auxiliary sense of taste — curiosity about ingenious and puzzling contrivances acts as a surrogate for pure aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objects designed to 'puzzle the beholder' and show ingenuity are valued not because of serviceability but because they indicate labor and expense. Anti-pattern: novelty that merely bewilders without implying costly workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon of conspicuous waste (pecuniary beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous waste: the expression of economic facility or serviceability by manifest, wasteful expenditure — pecuniary beauty — substitutes for or shapes aesthetic canons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canon selects for designs that evidence labor or expense beyond functional needs, and acts as a regulative, selective principle rather than an originator of innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective adaptation to expensiveness produces idiosyncrasies
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs become a congeries of idiosyncrasies under selective surveillance of the canon of expensiveness; idiosyncratic features are retained when they serve as marks of costliness or reputability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: variety driven by signaling cost rather than unified aesthetic progress. Example: architectural fronts and apartment-house facades with decorative but functionally superfluous elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of wasted ingenuity for true beauty/serviceability (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous waste often leads to suppression of elements that bear scrutiny as expressions of beauty or serviceability, being replaced by misspent ingenuity and conspicuous ineptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: domestic architecture, fancy work, apparel where expense replaces genuine aesthetic or utilitarian quality; such objects would not be tolerated absent prescriptive tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorific (indirect/invidious) utility as part of an object's worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods acquire a secondary or indirect utility as evidence of relative ability to pay; this honorific element becomes a necessary component of the consumer's sense of a 'better' grade of goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To appeal to cultivated taste, an article must contain some of this indirect utility. Even private-consumed goods are expected to show marks of conspicuous waste ('a modicum of indirect utility').

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of costliness with merit ('cheap and nasty')
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers habitually equate cost with worth; inexpensive goods are seen as dishonorable or unworthy ('cheap and nasty'), prompting insistence on some obvious costliness even in private consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxim examples: 'A cheap coat makes a cheap man.' This bias raises aggregate consumption costs and guides purchasing towards visibly costly goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible finish/workmanship valued over material sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasers are guided more by finish and workmanship (visible costliness) than by marks of substantial serviceability; goods must show appreciable labor spent on finish in addition to mechanical efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers thus add honorific finishes to goods to meet consumer expectations; anti-pattern: perfectly serviceable machine-made goods rejected for lacking visible marks of expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-wrought imperfection as honorific mark vs. machine perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand labor tends to be more wasteful and show imperfections; those visible imperfections become honorific marks distinguishing hand-wrought goods from more perfectly made machine products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The favorable margin of crudeness must not show bungling (evidence of low cost) nor be so narrow as to suggest machine precision (also low cost). This requires discriminating taste to value the right degree of imperfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial inferiority of machine products (social differentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine-made goods, despite superior adaptation of means to ends, are often held ceremonially inferior because they lack the honorific marks of hand labor and expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fuels movements valuing handicraft and 'crudity' (e.g., Ruskin, Morris) as socially and aesthetically preferable under current pecuniary norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous waste as selective/regulative principle (not creative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of conspicuous waste is mainly selective: it does not originate innovations but determines which innovations survive by requiring conformity to reputability standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus innovation must conform to wastefulness norms to persist; the law conserves forms fit for its purpose rather than generating new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary norm of dress: conspicuous waste
rubrics_metrics.description: The broad dominant norm in dress is conspicuous waste: apparel is primarily a vehicle to show expensive consumption rather than merely to protect the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: much apparel expenditure aims at respectable appearance and conforming to social standards; people may sacrifice comfort to appear well dressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary norm of dress: conspicuous leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress should make plain that the wearer is not engaged in productive labor; neatness and signs of non-involvement in manual work signal leisure-exemption and social worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: spotless linen, patent-leather shoes, walking-stick — these convey inability or exemption from manual labor and thus higher status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tertiary norm of dress: novelty/up-to-date fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress must be up to date; the imperative of dressing in the latest accredited manner, with fashions changing frequently, increases wasteful expenditure and reinforces conspicuous consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty, as a corollary of conspicuous waste, ensures garments serve only briefly and are regularly replaced; but the motive for constant change also ties back to the original adornment motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adorn­ment as the creative motive within waste constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations in fashion originate in the non-economic motive of adornment (search for more acceptable form/color/effect), but must pass the selective test of conspicuous waste to be adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore changes are driven by aesthetic aims but constrained by requirements of costliness and reputability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress signaling of non-productivity via design that impedes work (gendered criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain features of apparel are deliberately contrived to hamper useful exertion (e.g., women's skirts, long hair, corsets) so as to signal that the wearer does not perform productive labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veblen's strong claim: some feminine garments (corset) function economically as 'mutilation' reducing capacity for work; this is treated as an explicit design criterion for status signaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity/limited edition as guarantee of pecuniary distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited edition production (e.g., in book-making) operates as a guarantee that a product is scarce, therefore costly, thereby lending pecuniary distinction to its consumer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kelmscott Press and artisanal book-making use obsolete/hand methods, less legible formats, and limited runs to signal expense and elevate status despite reduced serviceability.
